name: Weighted average cost of capital
title: Weighted average cost of capital: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Understand WACC as a financing-weighted cost of capital, including market-value weights, after-tax debt cost and the limits of a single company-wide rate.
definition: Weighted average cost of capital is a financing-weighted rate combining the required costs of a company’s debt and equity capital. Its value depends on the financing weights, component costs and assumed tax treatment of debt interest.
explanation: The weights describe the financing mix: common equity, debt and any preferred stock each contribute their share of total financing value. They are not weights based on sales or operating assets. A company-wide WACC can summarize that mix under stated costs, but using it for a particular project requires a separate judgment about whether the project has comparable risk. An entered market value and an accounting book balance also describe different things; substituting one for the other should be identified as an approximation.
formula: WACC = (E/V) × Re + (D/V) × Rd × (1 − T) + (P/V) × Rp; V = E + D + P
formulaNote: E, D and P are compatible financing values; Re, Rd and Rp are their annual costs, and T is the assumed marginal tax rate. The preferred term is zero when no preferred stock is included. The tax factor applies only to debt in this model.

example.title: Debt and equity produce a 7.8% WACC
example.intro: Common equity $600,000 at 10%; debt $400,000 at 6%; assumed marginal tax rate 25%.
steps: Total financing = $1,000,000; equity weight 60%, debt weight 40%.
example.answer: The common-equity contribution is 6 percentage points and the debt contribution is 1.8 points.
example.assumptions: Enter compatible annual costs and same-date market values. Debt interest deductibility is an assumption, not a tax determination. This is a static financing worksheet; it does not fetch company data or choose a discount rate for a project.

pitfall.title: A financing average is not a universal project hurdle rate
pitfall.text: Projects with different risk, currencies or financing assumptions do not automatically share the same appropriate discount rate. WACC also changes when its inputs change; increasing debt while holding all component costs fixed is a sensitivity assumption, not an optimized capital structure.

name: Capital asset pricing model
title: Capital asset pricing model: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Learn how CAPM connects beta, systematic market risk and an equity risk premium to a modeled required return, with the rate inputs kept distinct.
definition: The capital asset pricing model links a modeled required return to exposure to systematic market risk, represented by beta. It adds a beta-scaled market risk premium to a compatible risk-free rate.
explanation: Beta measures the model’s exposure to market movements rather than every kind of uncertainty affecting a company. A market return includes the risk-free component; a market risk premium is the amount above that component. Entering one in a field intended for the other changes the estimate. CAPM describes a required-return relationship under its assumptions. It does not say that a future realized return will equal that estimate or that beta captures all business risks.
formula: Required return = Rf + β × (Rm − Rf) = Rf + β × ERP
formulaNote: Rf is the risk-free annual assumption, Rm the expected annual market return and ERP their difference. Beta has no percentage unit. Keep rate conventions, currency and the interpretation of the market assumptions compatible.

example.title: Market return of 9% gives a 5-point premium
example.intro: Risk-free annual rate 4%; expected market return 9%; beta 1.2.
example.assumptions: Annual assumptions only; no price-history beta regression or live market inputs. The output is one model of equity cost, not a forecast or investment recommendation. Negative beta and negative premiums are accepted within the stated input limits.

expected.label: CAPM required annual return / cost of equity

pitfall.title: A premium is not the total market return
pitfall.text: Subtracting the risk-free rate from an input that is already a market risk premium removes that component twice. The return-input and premium-input forms agree only when the inputs represent the same assumptions.

tools.text: Compare equivalent market-return and market-premium inputs.
Place an assumed equity cost alongside debt and preferred financing costs.

name: Bond duration
title: Bond duration: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Distinguish Macaulay duration, modified duration and maturity. Understand present-value timing weights and local bond-price sensitivity to a defined yield change.
definition: Bond duration summarizes the timing or yield sensitivity of a bond’s cash flows. Macaulay duration is a present-value-weighted payment time; modified duration converts it to a local price-sensitivity measure under a specified yield convention.
explanation: Maturity records the final payment date. Macaulay duration also accounts for earlier coupons, weighting each payment time by the payment’s present value as a share of total price. Modified duration answers a different question: the approximate proportional price response to a small yield change when the modeled cash flows stay fixed. DV01 expresses the first-order response to one basis point in money rather than as a percentage of price. These measures require a consistent yield and payment-frequency convention.
formula: Macaulay duration = Σ(tᵢ × PV(CFᵢ)) / price; modified duration = Macaulay duration / (1 + y/m)
formulaNote: Payment times tᵢ are in years, y is decimal nominal annual yield, and m is coupons per year in the regular-period model. Modified duration is a local approximation. Convexity adds a second-order term; an exact fixed-cash-flow comparison reprices every payment.

example.title: A ten-year semiannual 5% coupon bond
example.intro: Face $1,000; coupon 5%; nominal annual yield 6%; two coupons per year; 20 remaining periods; +1 percentage-point yield shock.
steps: Each regular coupon is $25; the final payment adds $1,000 principal.
Discount each payment by 1.03 raised to its coupon-period number. The price is $925.6126256977.
Weight each payment time by its share of price. Macaulay duration is 7.8949973402 years; divide by 1.03 for modified duration.
example.answer: Modified duration is 7.6650459613 years, convexity is 71.7853980129 years squared and DV01 is about $0.709486 per $1,000 face.
example.assumptions: Regular remaining coupon periods with settlement on a coupon date; nominal annual yield compounded at the coupon frequency. No accrued interest, irregular coupons, default or embedded-option model. Effective duration for rate-dependent cash flows is outside this worksheet.

pitfall.title: Long maturity and high duration are not interchangeable
pitfall.text: Payment timing and present-value weights matter, so final maturity alone does not determine duration. If cash flows can change with rates, as with some callable or mortgage-related instruments, fixed-cash-flow modified duration does not supply an effective-duration model.

tools.text: Inspect timing weights, local sensitivity and fixed-cash-flow repricing.
Explore bond price and yield under its separate payment assumptions.

name: CD early withdrawal penalty
title: CD early withdrawal penalty: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Understand CD early withdrawal penalties, including the contract rate and charge basis, accrued interest, and when a charge can reduce principal.
definition: A CD early withdrawal penalty is a contractual charge for removing funds from a certificate of deposit before its stated maturity. The applicable contract determines the charge basis, interest rate, penalty period and any minimum or exception.
explanation: A penalty stated as days or months of interest still needs a balance base, rate and time convention before it becomes a dollar amount. Those terms come from the agreement rather than a universal bank rule. Accrued interest and the penalty are separate: accrued interest adds to proceeds, while the charge subtracts from them. When the charge exceeds the included accrued interest, the modeled proceeds can fall below the entered principal. Other charges, withholding and bank-specific exceptions need separate treatment.
formula: Days: B × r × d / day basis; months: B × r × n / 12
formulaNote: User-entered contract parameters; no current bank-policy database or APY-to-contract-rate conversion. Accrued interest includes only interest paid with this withdrawal. Actual minimums, compound-interest rules, exceptions and partial-withdrawal policies need confirmation with the bank.

example.title: 90 days of contract interest on a 365-day basis
example.intro: Principal $10,000; unpaid accrued interest $200; contract annual rate 4.5%; 90 penalty days; 365-day basis.
example.answer: Net proceeds are $10,089.04 before any other charges or tax withholding.
example.assumptions: User-entered contract parameters; no current bank-policy database or APY-to-contract-rate conversion. Accrued interest includes only interest paid with this withdrawal. Actual minimums, compound-interest rules, exceptions and partial-withdrawal policies need confirmation with the bank.

pitfall.title: APY alone does not specify the penalty
pitfall.text: APY expresses earnings with a compounding convention. It does not identify the contract’s penalty rate, charge base or minimum. Read the withdrawal clause before converting a headline number of interest days into a charge.

name: Burn rate
title: Burn rate: Formula, Example & Limits
description: Define gross and net cash burn separately from accounting loss. Understand consistent operating-flow scope, cash reserves and the constant-rate runway relationship.
definition: Cash burn is the pace at which operating cash outflows consume available cash. Gross burn counts operating outflows; net burn offsets comparable operating inflows for the same period and classification scope.
explanation: Cash burn describes a flow over time, while a cash balance is a stock at a particular date. Runway relates the two under an assumed continuing net burn. A reserve changes the cash boundary used for that estimate; it does not change the operating burn itself. Borrowing, fundraising and other non-operating movements can change a balance without changing operating consumption. Two cash balances therefore need reconciliation before their difference can be interpreted as net operating burn, and that difference alone does not identify gross outflows.
formula: Gross burn = operating outflow; net burn = outflow − inflow
formulaNote: Use available cash and consistent operating cash-flow classifications. Balance-history mode requires removal of financing and all other excluded non-operating movements. It infers net operating burn only; gross outflows are not identifiable from two balances.

example.title: A cash reserve shortens usable runway
example.intro: Available cash $100,000; reserve $10,000; monthly operating outflows $25,000 and inflows $10,000.
steps: Gross burn = $25,000 per month. Net burn = $25,000 − $10,000 = $15,000.
Runway to reserve = $90,000 / $15,000 = 6 months; runway to zero = 6.666667 months.
example.answer: The reserve is reached after six modeled months, before cash reaches zero.
example.assumptions: Use available cash and consistent operating cash-flow classifications. Balance-history mode requires removal of financing and all other excluded non-operating movements. It infers net operating burn only; gross outflows are not identifiable from two balances.

pitfall.title: Accounting loss and cash burn can differ
pitfall.text: Accruals, noncash expenses and the timing of collections or payments separate accounting profit from cash movement. A runway based on constant burn is a scenario, not a forecast of future funding or a guarantee that every obligation can be paid.
